questions.question_text: Find $\int 12x^{3}\left(3x^{4}+5\right)^{2}dx$ using the substitution $u = 3x^{4}+5$. Give your answer in simplest form, with $+C$.

options.why: Raised the power of the bracket but did not divide by the new power $3$.
Divided by the new power and then divided by $12$ again, although the $12x^{3}$ was already used up in $du$.
Kept the factor $12x^{3}$ in the answer after it had already been absorbed into $du$.
Kept the original $x$ limits and substituted them into the expression in $u$.
Did not divide by the new power $4$ when integrating $u^{3}$.
Changed the limits using $u = x^{2}$ instead of $u = x^{2}-1$.
Omitted the factor $\dfrac{1}{2}$ that comes from $du = 2\cos 2x\,dx$.
Kept the $\dfrac{1}{2}$ but evaluated $\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)^{4}$ as $\dfrac{3}{4}$, squaring the surd once instead of raising it to the fourth power.
Omitted the factor $\dfrac{1}{2}$ and also evaluated $\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)^{4}$ as $\dfrac{3}{4}$.

questions.question_text: Find $\int x\sqrt{x+2}\,dx$ using the substitution $u = x+2$. Give your answer in simplest form, with $+C$.

options.why: Wrote $x = u+2$ instead of $x = u-2$, so the second term came out positive.
Integrated $-2u^{\frac{1}{2}}$ as $-\dfrac{2}{3}u^{\frac{3}{2}}$, dropping the factor $2$.
Made both slips: the wrong sign for $x$ in terms of $u$ and a dropped factor $2$.
Dropped the factor $\dfrac{1}{2}$ in $x = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(u^{2}-1\right)$.
Kept the original $x$ limits $0$ and $4$ instead of changing them to $u$ values.
Substituted only the upper limit and treated the lower limit as giving zero.

questions.solution_text:
$x = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(u^{2}-1\right)$, so $2x+1 = u^{2}$ and $\sqrt{2x+1} = u$
$\dfrac{dx}{du} = u$, so $dx = u\,du$
When $x = 0$, $u = 1$.
When $x = 4$, $u = 3$.
$\int_{0}^{4} \dfrac{x}{\sqrt{2x+1}}\,dx$
$= \int_{1}^{3} \dfrac{\frac{1}{2}\left(u^{2}-1\right)}{u} \times u\,du$
$= \dfrac{1}{2}\int_{1}^{3} \left(u^{2}-1\right)du$
$= \dfrac{1}{2}\left[\dfrac{u^{3}}{3} - u\right]_{1}^{3}$
$= \dfrac{1}{2}\left(6 + \dfrac{2}{3}\right)$
$= \dfrac{10}{3}$

questions.question_text: The integral $\int_{0}^{\ln 3} \dfrac{e^{2x}}{1+e^{2x}}\,dx$ is to be evaluated using the substitution $u = 1+e^{2x}$. Which integral in $u$ is correct?

options.why: Kept the original $x$ limits after changing the variable to $u$.
Omitted the factor $\dfrac{1}{2}$ that comes from $du = 2e^{2x}\,dx$.
Changed the limits using $u = e^{2x}$ instead of $u = 1+e^{2x}$.

questions.question_text: Find $\int \dfrac{\sin x}{3+\cos x}\,dx$ using the substitution $u = 3+\cos x$. Give your answer in simplest form, with $+C$.

options.why: Missed the negative sign coming from $du = -\sin x\,dx$.
Wrote the substitution as $u = 3-\cos x$, changing the sign inside the logarithm.
Wrote $u = 3-\cos x$ and also lost the negative sign from $du$.

questions.solution_text:
$u = 3+\cos x$
$\dfrac{du}{dx} = -\sin x$, so $\sin x\,dx = -du$
$\int \dfrac{\sin x}{3+\cos x}\,dx$
$= \int \dfrac{-1}{u}\,du$
$= -\ln u + C$
$= -\ln(3+\cos x) + C$

questions.question_text: The gradient of a curve is $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{6x}{\left(x^{2}+3\right)^{2}}$ and the curve passes through the point $(1,\,2)$. Using the substitution $u = x^{2}+3$, find $y$ as a function of $x$.

options.why: Took $C$ to be the $y$-value of the point instead of solving for it.
Lost the negative sign when integrating $u^{-2}$, which also changes the constant.
Did not use $du = 2x\,dx$, so the coefficient stayed at $6$ instead of becoming $3$.

questions.question_text: Evaluate $\int_{0}^{3} \dfrac{x}{\sqrt{x+1}}\,dx$ using the substitution $x = u^{2}-1$, where $u \ge 0$.

options.why: Omitted the factor $2$ from $dx = 2u\,du$.
Kept the original $x$ limits $0$ and $3$ instead of changing them to the $u$ values $1$ and $2$.
Forgot that $\sqrt{x+1}=u$ sits in the denominator and integrated $\left(u^{2}-1\right)\times 2u$ instead of $\dfrac{u^{2}-1}{u}\times 2u$.

questions.solution_text:
$x = u^{2}-1$, so $x+1 = u^{2}$ and $\sqrt{x+1} = u$
$\dfrac{dx}{du} = 2u$, so $dx = 2u\,du$
When $x = 0$, $u = 1$.
When $x = 3$, $u = 2$.
$\int_{0}^{3} \dfrac{x}{\sqrt{x+1}}\,dx$
$= \int_{1}^{2} \dfrac{u^{2}-1}{u} \times 2u\,du$
$= 2\int_{1}^{2} \left(u^{2}-1\right)du$
$= 2\left[\dfrac{u^{3}}{3} - u\right]_{1}^{2}$
$= 2\left(\dfrac{2}{3} - \left(-\dfrac{2}{3}\right)\right)$
$= \dfrac{8}{3}$

options.why: Omitted the factor $\dfrac{1}{2}$ from $x\,dx = -\dfrac{1}{2}du$.
Left the limits reversed as $1$ to $0$ as well as using the negative from $-\dfrac{1}{2}du$.
Replaced $x^{3}\,dx$ by $-\dfrac{1}{2}du$, forgetting that $x^{2} = 1-u$ still has to be substituted.
